causalMechanism.primaryVector: Surgical peritoneal-injury sequence: opening the peritoneal cavity causes mesothelial injury, local ischemia at the operative site, and an inflammatory exudate of fibrinogen that is converted to fibrin. When the peritoneal fibrinolytic capacity is overwhelmed — as it is in the days after laparotomy — the fibrinous bridges are not lysed but become organized by fibroblast in-growth and angiogenesis into permanent collagenous adhesions that tether bowel to the abdominal wall, the liver bed, or adjacent viscera. Those bands cause traction, kinking, and mesenteric distortion that can produce intermittent partial obstruction with colicky pain, nausea, vomiting, and constipation, and can progress to complete small bowel obstruction or internal herniation requiring emergency surgery; each subsequent adhesiolysis creates new peritoneal injury and new adhesions, so the process is self-reinforcing. Ellis et al. (PMID 10232313), a retrospective cohort using Scottish National Health Service record-linkage data, found that 34.6 percent of 29,790 patients who underwent open abdominal or pelvic surgery in a single year were readmitted a mean of 2.1 times over 10 years for a disorder that could be directly or possibly linked to adhesions, and that nearly a fifth of those readmissions were directly attributable to adhesions. Tingstedt et al. (PMID 17330836) followed 102 patients operated for adhesion-caused small bowel obstruction with a median follow-up of about 14 years and reported long-term readmission and cost outcomes, finding a higher readmission rate than previously reported. Lorentzen et al. (PMID 29030779) reviewed patients requiring emergency surgery for adhesive small bowel obstruction and found an overall recurrence rate of about 12 percent, with risk persisting for years after the index operation. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory, in which a disability resulting from surgery performed to treat the service-connected cholelithiasis is itself proximately due to that service-connected condition, so the cholelithiasis that necessitated the cholecystectomy is the legal and medical predicate for adhesions produced by that operation. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows pre-existing peritoneal adhesions from earlier abdominal surgery, endometriosis, or intra-abdominal infection and the claim is that the new operation measurably worsened a baseline adhesive burden, in which case the new-surgery increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing adhesions and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: documentation of the service-connected cholelithiasis; the operative note establishing that an open cholecystectomy was performed and describing the peritoneal field; an interval during which obstruction symptoms appear after the operation rather than before it; and objective findings of adhesive obstruction or tethering — imaging showing a transition point, adhesions at reoperation, or operative findings of bands — rather than pain alone. Only then can an examiner state that the peritoneal adhesions are at least as likely as not caused by the open cholecystectomy performed for the service-connected cholelithiasis — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Two candid limitations must be disclosed. First, the strength of this theory depends on the surgical approach: laparoscopic cholecystectomy carries a substantially lower adhesion-related readmission risk than open surgery, so a laparoscopic operation weakens but does not automatically defeat the claim, and the operative report is decisive. Second, adhesions are a common incidental finding in any patient who has undergone abdominal surgery, so the nexus opinion must link the specific symptom pattern to documented adhesive obstruction rather than to coexisting conditions. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include other surgical and non-surgical causes of bowel obstruction (hernia, malignancy, Crohn's disease, gallstone ileus, bezoars), irritable bowel syndrome and chronic constipation, gastroparesis, chronic cholecystitis and post-cholecystectomy syndrome, endometriosis, prior surgery in any quadrant, and peritonitis or abscess from the index episode. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14 and the anti-pyramiding instruction of § 4.114: the same abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and constipation may not be compensated simultaneously under the cirrhosis, gastropathy, or post-cholecystectomy codes and again under the adhesion code, and where more than one rating is warranted under DCs 7301 through 7329 the schedule requires a single evaluation reflecting the predominant disability picture.

Primary condition: Service-connected cholelithiasis requiring cholecystectomy, performed as an open procedure
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7315 (cholelithiasis, chronic) rated as DC 7314 (chronic biliary tract disease): 30 percent with three or more clinically documented attacks of right-upper-quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting in the past 12 months or requiring biliary stricture dilatation at least once in the past 12 months; 10 percent with one or two such attacks; 0 percent if asymptomatic without a documented attack; with DC 7318 for complications of cholecystectomy such as strictures and biliary leaks
Secondary condition: Peritoneal adhesions (post-surgical adhesive disease with recurrent or intermittent small bowel obstruction) following open cholecystectomy for service-connected cholelithiasis
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7301 (peritoneum, adhesions of, due to surgery, trauma, disease, or infection): 80 percent for persistent partial bowel obstruction that is inoperable and refractory to treatment or requires total parenteral nutrition; 50 percent for symptomatic adhesions persisting or recurring after surgery with documented dietary modification and clinical evidence of recurrent obstruction requiring hospitalization at least once a year plus at least one of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, colic, constipation, or diarrhea; 30 percent for the same symptomatic pattern without the hospitalization requirement; 10 percent for symptomatic adhesions with at least one of those symptoms; 0 percent for history of adhesions currently asymptomatic. Qualified-human rating review required
Original nexus theory: Causation
